why: The core pointer exercise every other linked-list problem builds on: walk the list once, turning each next pointer around while remembering the node you came from.
hints: When you point cur.next backwards, you lose the rest of the list. Save it first.
Keep prev (initially None) and cur (initially head). Each step: nxt = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt.
When cur becomes None, prev is the new head. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) extra space; avoid recursion, since 10^5 nodes overflows Python's stack.
pitfalls: Empty list: return None without touching anything.
Recursive reversal hits the recursion limit for 10^5 nodes.
Return prev, not cur (cur is None at the end).
statement:
You are given head, the first node of a finite, acyclic singly linked list (each node has val and next). Reverse the list in place by turning every next pointer around, and return the new head. Use the original nodes; do not build new ones. Return None for an empty list.

Worked example. 1 -> 2 -> 3

  • Start: prev = None, cur = 1.
  • Node 1 now points to None; prev = 1, cur = 2.
  • Node 2 now points to 1; prev = 2, cur = 3.
  • Node 3 now points to 2; prev = 3, cur = None. Stop.
  • Return node 3: the list reads 3 -> 2 -> 1.
